e: Old French abatre (to beat down), from Latin ad + battuere (to beat).
t: « Abattre »: the storm is beaten down. The storm abated.
Acus = needle: a mind sharp as a point. Business acumen = le sens des affaires.

m: To make impure by adding inferior substances.
t: Adding something other (alter): watered-down wine is adulterated, « frelaté ».
Levis = léger: alleviate = « alléger » the pain.

e: Latin approbatio, from approbare (to approve): ad + probare (to test, find good).
t: Same as « approbation ». Opposite: opprobrium.

m: Expressing oneself clearly; to express clearly.
e: Latin articulatus (jointed), from articulus (small joint). Speech divided into distinct parts.
t: Joints (articulations) make movement clear; articulate speech is clearly jointed.

m: To state or assert to be true.
t: Aver = declare it « avéré », true (verus).

m: High-sounding but with little meaning; pompous.
e: From bombast, cotton padding for clothes, from Medieval Latin bombax (cotton). Padded speech.
t: Bombast = cotton stuffing: speech padded with fluff.
French « chicane »: legal tricks and quibbles.
Same as « circonspect »: looking all around before acting.

m: A loud, insistent demand or noise.
t: « Une clameur »: the crowd shouting for something.

e: From comply, Italian complire, from Latin complere (to fill up, complete).
t: Compliant with the rules = « conforme ». Compliance team.

m: An expert judge in matters of taste.
t: Straight from French « connaisseur ».

e: Old French covert (covered), past participle of covrir (to cover).
t: Covered = « couvert ». Covert ops. Opposite: overt (ouvert).
Siccus = sec: « dessécher ».
Frighten away (terrere, as in terreur). Nuclear deterrent = « force de dissuasion ».
Feeling apart: a dissenting opinion. « Dissension ».

m: To deprive or rid oneself of something.
t: Un-dress: divesting a business unit = taking off a piece of clothing (vêtement).

m: The ability to produce the intended result.
t: « Efficacité » of a drug in a clinical trial.
Same as « éloquent »: speaking out.

m: A perfect example of a type.
t: Once a summary; now the essence condensed. Not « épitomé » (summary) in modern use.

m: A speech praising someone, especially at a funeral.
t: Eu-logos = speaking well of someone. « Éloge ».
Unfolded fully. Opposite: implicit (folded in).
Same as « faciliter ».
Boiling: same root as « ferveur ».

e: Old French guile (deceit), probably Frankish; related to English wile.
t: Guile = wiles = ruse. Guileless = without it.

e: From gull (to dupe), perhaps from the seagull, a bird that swallows anything.
t: A seagull swallows whatever is thrown. « Crédule ».
Same as « homogène ».

m: Implied though not stated; absolute (implicit trust).
t: Folded inside. Opposite: explicit.
Nothing follows from it: no consequences.
No boundary drawn: « indéterminé ».
Can’t be handled or pulled (tractor). An intractable problem.

e: Old French lavasse (downpour), from laver (to wash). A flood of something.
t: A downpour (« lavasse ») of gifts. Lavish praise.
Same as « loquace ».
« Naissant »: just born. A nascent industry.
Onus = burden. French « onéreux » means expensive; English onerous means heavy work.
Same as « jeter l’opprobre sur ». Opposite of approbation.

e: Old French overt (open), past participle of ovrir (to open), now ouvrir.
t: Overt = « ouvert ». Covert = « couvert ».

m: A seemingly self-contradictory statement that may be true.
t: Against common opinion (doxa). Same as « paradoxe ».

m: Strongly biased towards a party or cause.
t: Same as « partisan »: taking one party’s side.
« Pléthore de candidats »: an overflow.

m: Conformity to accepted standards of behaviour.
e: Old French propriete, from Latin proprietas (appropriateness), from proprius (one’s own, proper).
t: Not property! Propriety = « les convenances », what is proper.
Same as « tacite »: « reconduction tacite ».

e: Latin tangentem, from tangere (to touch). A tangent only touches the circle at one point.
t: Going off on a tangent: barely touching the topic. « Partir dans une digression ».
Same as « ténu »: a thin thread of logic.
Same as « véracité ». Vrai.
Same as « verbeux »: too many verbs/words.

m: Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably.
t: Flying away (voler): volatile markets, a volatile temper.

e: Old English wær (watchful). Germanic, related to aware and beware.
t: Beware → wary. Méfiant.

m: Having great energy for a cause.
t: Same as « zélé ». Zealots were fervent rebels in Judea.
